questions.q: Which of these is not a reason the lesson gives for writing functions?
questions.explain: Functions are about reuse, clear names and testing. They do not make code faster than a loop; a function often contains a loop.
options: Write a piece of logic once and reuse it
Give the logic a name that says what it does
Test the logic on its own
Make the code run faster than a loop

questions.q: What does it mean to call a function?
questions.explain: Running a function is calling it. You write the name followed by parentheses with the arguments.
options: To write its definition with the function keyword
To run it, for example with formatTask("Buy milk", true)
To store it in a variable

questions.q: In function formatTask(title, done) { … } and the call formatTask("Buy milk", true), what are title and done?
questions.explain: Parameters are the names in the definition. Arguments are the actual values in the call: "Buy milk" and true.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first argument goes to the first parameter, whatever its name. So title is true and done is "Buy milk", which is truthy.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: logTask prints, but it has no return, so it gives back undefined. Printing and returning are different things.
options:
Task: Buy milk
Task: Buy milk

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A parameter without an argument is undefined. Extra arguments are ignored. JavaScript does not throw for either.

questions.q: Why is a function that returns a value usually more useful than one that prints it?
questions.explain: A returned value can be used in many ways. A function that only prints forces one use, and makes testing harder.
options: Printing is not allowed inside functions
The caller decides what to do with the value: print it, save it or send it
Returned values are faster to compute
A function that prints cannot have parameters

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function is a value, so it can be stored in a variable. That is a function expression. typeof reports it as "function".

questions.q: This arrow function has braces but no return. What does it print?
questions.explain: With braces, the body is a block and needs return, like a normal function. Without it, the function returns undefined. Drop the braces or add return.

questions.q: How do you write an arrow function with no parameters that returns "Hello!"?
questions.explain: No parameters means empty parentheses (). A single-expression body is returned without the return keyword.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Function declarations are hoisted: JavaScript sets them up before running the other lines, so you can call them before the line where they are written.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function stored in a const is not hoisted like a declaration. It cannot be used before the line that sets it has run.

questions.q: Which habit does the lesson describe for choosing between the two styles?
questions.explain: Both styles are fine. The common habit is declarations for the main functions and short arrows for callbacks.
options: Always use arrow functions; declarations are outdated
function declarations for a file's main named functions, arrow functions for short functions passed to other functions
Declarations only inside loops, arrow functions everywhere else
Arrow functions only when they have more than one parameter

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A default is used when the argument is missing. When you pass a value, it replaces the default.

questions.q: A default parameter is used when the argument is missing or undefined. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only undefined (or a missing argument) triggers the default. null is a real value you passed, so it is used as it is.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The rest parameter collects all the arguments into an array. With no arguments it is an empty array, so the loop never runs and the total stays 0.

questions.q: Which function definition is valid?
questions.explain: The rest parameter collects everything that is left, so it must be the last parameter, and there can be only one.

questions.q: What is a callback?
questions.explain: Because functions are values, you can pass one to another function. The receiving function "calls it back". A function that calls itself is recursion.
options: A function you pass as an argument to another function, which calls it when needed
A function declared at the top of a file

questions.q: What makes a function a higher-order function?
questions.explain: repeat(times, action) takes a function, and multiplier(factor) returns one. Both are higher-order functions.
options: It is declared with the function keyword
It takes a function as an argument or returns a function
It has more than two parameters

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: repeat decides how often; the callback says what to do. It is called with i = 1, then 2.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Any function can be a callback, including a built-in like Math.round. results.push adds each result to the end of the array.

questions.q: You want to pass Math.round as a callback to applyToAll. Which call is correct?
questions.explain: Pass the function itself, without parentheses. Math.round() would call it straight away and pass its result (NaN) instead of the function.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: multiplier returns a new function each time. triple remembers factor = 3, and half remembers 0.5.

questions.q: Which function is pure?
questions.explain: A pure function gives the same result for the same arguments and changes nothing outside itself. Changing total and printing are side effects, and Math.random() gives a different result each time.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: addToTotal changes a variable outside itself, so the same call gives different results. That is why it is impure and harder to test.

questions.q: A backend must save data to a database, which is a side effect. What habit does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: A backend cannot be pure everywhere, but pure logic is easy to test and trust. Keep side effects few and in clear places, like the thin keyboard part of the guessing game.
options: Make every function impure, since pure functions cannot be used in a backend
Keep the logic in pure functions and the side effects in a few clear places
Put the database code inside every function that needs it
Avoid databases and keep everything in variables

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function can read variables from outside, like appName. But prefix exists only inside makeTitle. typeof on a name that does not exist gives "undefined" instead of throwing.
options:
[Tasks] Buy milk
ReferenceError: prefix is not defined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call to createCounter makes a new, separate count. The returned function remembers its own count even after createCounter finished. That is a closure.

questions.q: What is a closure?
questions.explain: A closure keeps access to the variables of the place where it was created, even after that outer function has finished.
options: A function that closes the program when it finishes
A function that remembers the variables around the place where it was created
The closing brace of a function body

questions.q: In createCounter, how can code outside change count?
questions.explain: Nothing outside can reach count directly. That makes closures a simple way to keep data private. Calling createCounter() again makes a new, separate counter.
options: Only by calling the returned function, which adds one

questions.q: What happens when a recursive function has no base case?
questions.explain: The base case is where the function stops calling itself and just returns. Without it, the calls never stop until the call stack is full.
options: It returns undefined after the first call
It keeps calling itself until JavaScript stops it with "Maximum call stack size exceeded"
JavaScript adds a base case automatically

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: factorial(4) is 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. For 1 and 0, the base case n <= 1 returns 1 straight away.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The project has 2 direct subtasks, and the first one has 1 more: 3 in total. A task with no subtasks is the base case: the loop runs zero times and returns 0.

questions.q: Where does recursion fit better than a simple loop?
questions.explain: Recursion shines on nested data: each subtask is handled by the same function. Flat lists and counting are simpler with loops.
options: Data that contains smaller copies of itself, like tasks with subtasks or folders with folders
Printing each item of a flat list

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Three dots in a call spread an array out into separate arguments, the opposite of a rest parameter. sum(values.length) just passes the number 3.

questions.q: The calculator throws Not a number: 2 for calculator.add("2", 3). Why is that better than returning a result?
questions.explain: With a string, + joins text instead of adding. A silent wrong answer is worse than a clear error, so the library checks its inputs first.
options: Because throwing is faster than adding
Because "2" + 3 would silently give "23"; bad input should be refused loudly
Because add can only return whole numbers
Because strings cannot be passed to functions

questions.q: Every calculator function first calls requireNumbers. What is the benefit?
questions.explain: Putting a check used by many functions in one helper avoids copying it. When the rule changes, you fix one place.
options: The shared check is written, and fixed, in one place
It turns strings into numbers automatically

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: check runs the callback inside try, so a thrown error becomes a result instead of a crash. The float test fails because 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3.
options:
PASS divide -> 3
PASS zero -> error: Cannot divide by zero
FAIL float -> 0.30000000000000004

PASS divide -> 3
FAIL zero -> error: Cannot divide by zero
FAIL float -> 0.30000000000000004

PASS divide -> 3
PASS zero -> error: Cannot divide by zero
PASS float -> 0.3

PASS divide -> 3
Error: Cannot divide by zero

questions.q: Why does check(label, run, expected) take a callback run instead of the result value?
questions.explain: If you passed calculator.divide(1, 0) directly, it would throw before check even started. Passing () => calculator.divide(1, 0) lets check call it inside try.
options: Because values cannot be compared with ===
So it can run the code inside try and report a thrown error instead of crashing

questions.q: Finish the function declaration formatTask(title, done) so it returns [x] TITLE when done is true and [ ] TITLE otherwise.
questions.explain: Choose the mark with a ternary and return the string; the caller prints it.

questions.q: Write two arrow functions without braces: power(base, exponent) using **, and remainder(a, b) using %. The program should print 1024 2.
questions.explain: A single-expression arrow function returns its value automatically: (a, b) => a % b.
questions.starter:
// write power and remainder here

console.log(power(2, 10), remainder(17, 5));

questions.q: Finish greet using default parameters: name defaults to "friend" and greeting to "Hello". It returns GREETING, NAME!.
questions.explain: Write the default after = in the parameter list. It is used when the argument is missing.
questions.expected:
Hello, Ada!
Hello, friend!
Welcome back, Ada!

questions.q: Finish largest with a rest parameter and a loop: return the biggest number passed, or null when no numbers are passed. The program should print 9 -1 null.
questions.explain: The rest parameter ...numbers is always an array, empty when nothing is passed. Start from the first number, not from 0, or negative lists give the wrong answer.

questions.q: Finish multiplier(factor) so it returns a function that multiplies its argument by factor. The program should print 30 5.
questions.explain: Return an arrow function. It remembers factor from the call that created it, which is a closure.

questions.q: Finish createCounter(start) with a closure. It returns a function; each call adds one to a private count that begins at start, and returns the new count. The program should print 11 12 1.
questions.explain: Keep count in a let inside the outer function. The returned arrow function changes it; each counter has its own count.

questions.q: Write a recursive countdown(n) that returns a string like "3 2 1 go". For 0 or less it returns "go" (the base case).
questions.explain: The base case n <= 0 stops the calls. Using <= also protects you from a negative start, which would never reach 0.

questions.q: Finish divide(a, b). Throw new Error("Not a number") when either value is not a number (strings and NaN count as bad), throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero") when b is 0, and otherwise return a / b.
questions.explain: Validate the inputs first and refuse bad ones loudly. typeof NaN is "number", so you need Number.isNaN as well.
questions.expected:
3
error: Cannot divide by zero
error: Not a number
error: Not a number

questions.q: Finish the higher-order function repeat(times, action) so it calls the callback action with 1, 2, … up to times.
questions.explain: repeat owns the loop; the callback decides what happens each time. Call it with action(i).

questions.q: 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false. Write a pure arrow function closeTo(a, b) that returns true when the two numbers differ by less than 0.000001. The program should print true false.
questions.explain: Compare decimals by checking that their difference is tiny. Math.abs makes the difference positive, whichever number is bigger. Test runners do the same, for example Vitest's toBeCloseTo.
questions.solution:
const closeTo = (a, b) => Math.abs(a - b) < 0.000001;

console.log(closeTo(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3), closeTo(0.3, 0.4));
